sentence: We re-tested the main claims of new robot-learning papers on an SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX.
The pieces cost €1,350 and the compute $45.10.
Each re-test ran the cheapest baseline first, and its pass mark was committed before the run.
Of the 37 paper claims we tested, 12 were valid on our hardware.

Three proposed classes cover the failures: edge latency (a method misses the real-time budget on the edge GPU), zero-shot judges (a judge loses to a trivial signal) and latent planners (a planner loses to the commanded joints).
A blind second reader still has to confirm the classes.
We also verified our own pre-registration by commit history.
For most gates the order of bar and result can be read from the repository, and for some it cannot.
Most of the 22 papers in this study were shown on setups far from ours.
9 were shown in simulation and 7 on rigs above X5k, which is where our rig falls.
The appendix table gives the rig of each paper, including the 3 in between and the 1 that does not say.
Our rig is an SO-101 arm and a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB.
Here is one entry.
An adaptive chunking paper claims that choosing the chunk length from the entropy of sampled chunks follows the task's phases, long in transport and short at the grasp.
On our edge GPU one such decision takes 4,751 ms.
The budget is 298 ms.
The entry records a fail on this rig.
It says nothing about the method on the hardware it was shown on.
Next to the verdict, the entry keeps the claim in the paper's words, our pass mark, our measurement and the published rows.
For each claim we first run the cheapest signal the learned model has to beat, on the same rows.
For a predictor this is copy-last.
For a latent it is the commanded joints.
For a judge it is episode length.
A gate's pass mark had to be in version control before its result.
Notes and commit dates can be edited by hand.
Commit ancestry cannot be changed without rewriting history that others have already cloned.
For each gate we find the first commit that contains its bar and the first that contains its result, and compare them (X, abridged):
Table 1 gives the classes for the 89 gates logged by 2026-10-31.
Most are bar-first and 0 are result-first.
A same-commit gate is one where bar and result entered the repository together.
It says nothing about which was written first.
Our first pass used text search and found 31 same-commit gates.
The cause was batch logging.
We traced each same-commit gate back to the earlier file that holds its bar.
This moved 21 gates to bar-first and 4 to no-bar, because their bar cell declares none.
6 stayed same-commit.
The audit table in the repository gives the evidence line for every move.
We did not re-audit the gates that were already bar-first.
One open candidate remains, the reward-model progress test of 2026-11-01.
It is same-commit by text search, although its protocol (X) is older than the log commit.
The early gates mixed point estimates and different intervals.
We recomputed 10 of them from stored rows with one statistic, the episode bootstrap (2,000 resamples, percentile 95 % CI).
For 3 of them the bar falls inside the interval (Table 2).
The colour judge is a fail on the point estimate, and its interval does not settle it.
The false-intervention threshold was fitted to meet its rate, so that interval is only descriptive.
The register keeps the pre-registered point verdicts and marks these three as fragile.
The cold reruns start from a fresh clone with no credentials.
6 gates reran and matched, 5 of them exactly.
12 more stop at the world-model environment, which is not published yet.
Publishing it would unblock most of them.
The remaining 11 need a larger GPU, a private checkpoint, the arm or a step the write-up leaves out.
We checked the register's citations and paper-side fields against the papers' PDFs and corrected them.
The register names 38 arXiv ids.
The ones missing from our papers mirror all belong to scheduled tests.
One tested paper has no arXiv id and was not checked against a PDF.
Table 3 counts the verdicts by paper and by claim row.
On claims taken from papers, 12 of 37 reproduce and 18 fail.
The other 8 rows test our own baselines, for example that the commanded joints beat the world model.
5 of those hold.
In other entries a model judged outcomes without training on this rig.
A learned reward model detects failures at AUROC 0.818.
Episode length alone reaches 0.938.
Judges of success, failure or progress that lose to a trivial signal like this form class B. Class C is about learned latents.
A world model ranks the executed chunk first in 0.60 of anchors.
Its pass mark was 0.8, and an action-only baseline reaches 0.68–0.90.
Class C holds latents used to plan, rank or track progress that lose to the joints, to copy-last or to an action-only baseline.
These examples illustrate the classes.
They do not count them.
A protocol committed before any labelling sets the rule for counting.
The labels count only once a blind second reader labels the same 20 failed rows on the same form and agrees with the first reading at Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6.
That reading has not happened yet.
One operator, the author, ran the rig and labelled the outcomes.
Labels were given at rest and not always blind to the arm.
Observer bias is therefore the main confound.
Where commit order shows it, the pass mark predates the run, so a label could not move the bar.
A blind two-reader protocol for the failure classes is committed.
It has not run yet, so no verdict has a second reader.
For 29 of the 89 gates the repository cannot show whether bar or result came first.
21 of the bar-first verdicts rest on matching a bar text in an earlier file.
Under the bootstrap 3 verdicts are fragile.
Cold reruns cover 6 gates so far, and the unpublished world-model environment blocks most of the rest.
A failure here describes this rig, not the paper in its own setting.
The papers were chosen for one stack, so the rate describes this register and not the field.
Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies.
A standardized real-world benchmark reports a taxonomy of failures and recoveries for VLA policies [arXiv:2606.08881].
A fleet of SO-101 cells evaluates policies at scale [arXiv:2607.24481].
The vla-eval tool runs VLAs across 14 simulation benchmarks [arXiv:2603.13966].
A benchmark of demonstration quality studies one method family [arXiv:2610.18869].
We test the claims behind methods (judges, world models, latency) against thresholds fixed before the run, and we audit our own pre-registration.
RoboSeed [arXiv:2610.40026] is the closest work.
It scores VLA and world-action models on five dimensions, including reproduction evidence and deployment affordability.
Its reproduction-evidence score counts five audit milestones (configuration mapping, task records, task coverage, training records, seeds).
Its authors state that this score is not a probability that a result is correct.
We give one pass or fail per claim on a €1,350 rig.
We re-tested 37 paper claims, and 12 held.
The rig cost €1,350 and the compute $45.10.
Every row behind the verdicts is published.
Our own history cannot show the order of bar and result for 29 of 89 gates.
If you re-test a paper on a cheap rig, run its cheapest baseline on the same rows first and commit the threshold before the run.
Every number here can be rebuilt from the repository (X).
We trained a small JEPA world model in the LeWorldModel recipe for $3.30 of rented GPU time.
The training data are teleoperated demonstrations of one tabletop task on an SO-101 arm.
We then re-tested on this model the uses of such models that recent papers propose.
Each use has a threshold in a public register.
We tested the encoder on policy rollouts the model never saw.
A linear probe on its last-frame latent separates success from failure about as well as a hand-built colour judge.
It does better than a frozen DINOv2 encoder and better than the commanded joints.
The predictor adds nothing to this.
At the grasp, the imagined latent reads the outcome at 0.70 and the current latent at 0.82.
Every use that needs the predictor to roll forward misses its threshold at this data scale.
The controls are exploratory and come from one rig and one model.
LeWorldModel (LeWM) trains a world model in two parts.
The encoder maps camera frames to a latent vector.
The predictor takes the current latent and a sequence of actions and imagines the latents that follow.
Both are trained together from pixels with a joint-embedding predictive (JEPA) loss.
Papers built on these models propose several uses.
Most of them need the predictor.
One ranks a policy's candidate action chunks by their imagined outcome.
Others flag a failure when the observed latent drifts from the predicted one, read the outcome of a grasp before it happens, or plan over several time scales.
Each paper reports the use that worked on its own robot and data.
We had one such model, trained on our own arm.
We ran every use we could find on it.
Each re-test is a row of a register with a threshold, a dataset, a result and a verdict.
Where we managed it, the threshold and the decision rule went into the repository before the result existed.
That commit order is what we mean by pre-registration.
All 20 rows match a pre-registration record in the commit history.
In 19 of them the bar was in place before the result.
The two-level hierarchical progress use had it in the same commit.
One more row is not a use of our model.
It times the pretrained RoboJEPA and V-JEPA 2.1 encoders on our on-board computer.
14 of the 20 rows fail or are no-go.
Table @tab:register lists all of them.
The first version of this paper argued something completely different.
We read the failures as a sign that the latent mostly encodes the arm's pose.
Then a frozen image encoder or the commanded joints would do at least as well.
We ran these controls on 69 policy rollouts.
The encoder read how the episode went better than either control.
We modified the claim around the predictor.
The controls came after the data.
Each readout is a linear probe with leave-one-session-out (LOSO) cross-validation on the 69 rollouts (44 success, 25 failure, 13 sessions).
The labels were given at rest by the author.
The model was trained on teleoperation only and never saw these rollouts.
No threshold was committed for these comparisons.
Everything this paper says about the split between encoder and predictor is therefore exploratory.
3 of the 3 register passes have their bar committed before the result.
The register still marks the outcome-readout verdict as retrospective.
The robot is one SO-101 arm driven through LeRobot, with a top and a wrist camera.
The task is to put a bowl into another bowl.
We trained our model on X, split by grid layout into 157 training and 25 validation episodes.
The evaluation rollouts come from a separate dataset, X. They are SmolVLA runs recorded after our model was trained.
Our model follows the LeWM recipe, with a multi-view ViT encoder, an action-conditioned predictor and the SIGReg regulariser.
We compare it with four cheaper signals.
The frozen DINOv2-S control is a frozen DINOv2 small encoder, mean-pooled over the top and wrist views as in DINO-WM.
The joints control is the commanded joint vector.
The colour judge is a hand-built rule on the final frame with no learning.
Policy identity is the checkpoint that ran the episode.
In October we found a loading bug.
A timing test on the on-board computer loaded our checkpoint with X. The image had transformers 5.5.4, and under that version 192 encoder tensors did not match.
They were dropped without an error, so the test timed a random encoder.
We voided its latents.
We then traced how every other use loaded the model.
26 ran the trained model and 1 ran a random one (that test).
The world-model block of VLA-JEPA, which one diagnostic below uses, loads all 351 of its keys.
Among the encoder uses, reading the outcome works.
The outcome readout at rest passes.
At the grasp anchor the current latent reads the grasp at 0.82.
Reading progress does not work.
Four uses ask the latent for progress or task stage, and all four fail.
They are progress monotonicity, two-level hierarchical progress, the latent stage tracker and SURVEYOR's latent-distance scale.
We also ran the pose probes of LeJEPA.
A linear readout recovers about half of the joint variance from our encoder (R² 0.565).
It recovers more from the frozen DINOv2-S control (0.867).
The predictor does predict its own latent.
At K = 30 its open-loop error is 0.31.
Copying the last latent gives 0.89.
The uses of this prediction fail.
In chunk ranking the model puts the executed chunk first in 0.60 of anchors.
The threshold was 0.8.
The commanded actions alone reach 0.68–0.90.
The surprise monitor catches 2/8 at 2/42 failures.
The hierarchical planner, the conformal surprise band, re-ranking, the risk head and the calibrated reflex also miss their thresholds.
Table @tab:register gives the margins.
We tested whether the encoder carries anything that a frozen encoder or the joints do not.
Table @tab:controls sets our model beside the four other signals on the same 69 rollouts.
Every probe is a LOSO linear probe against the author's labels.
At rest the interval is a 95 % episode-bootstrap CI.
At the anchor it is a bootstrap of the mean over 5 seeds of the out-of-fold AUROC, with episodes resampled jointly across the seeds (2,000 resamples, percentile).
At rest our model is level with the colour judge.
The two CIs overlap.
Our model is above the frozen encoder and the joints.
At the grasp anchor no judge applies, and our model is above both controls.
The pose probes hold the joints better than our encoder does.
They hold the outcome worse.
On these rollouts the encoder has outcome information that the pose alone does not give.
The anchor column depends on how the five seeds are combined.
If we average the predictions before scoring, our model gets 0.8377, frozen DINOv2-S 0.7175 and the joints 0.5346.
With seed 0 alone they get 0.7554, 0.7024 and 0.5574.
The gap to the frozen encoder is smaller with seed 0.
The order is the same.
On SURVEYOR's scale check the controls do better than our model.
Frozen DINOv2-S has τ 0.3601 and the joints τ 0.0265, and both pass.
Our model has τ 1.2488 and fails.
SURVEYOR reports 0.20.
The task and the rollouts are the same for all three features.
We take the failure as a property of our latent space.
ContactGuard finds that probes on the imagined latent beat probes on the current latent for grasp tasks.
We expected the same at our grasp anchor.
The pre-registered threshold asked the imagined latent for ≥ 0.85, ≥ +0.05 over the current one.
We find the reverse.
With the same encoder and the same anchor, the current latent reads the outcome at 0.82 and the imagined latent at 0.70.
The row fails.
We also ran the distillation probe on our model's inverse-dynamics term, pooled over the 25 teleoperation validation episodes.
The trained model scores 0.7476.
Its random initialisation scores 0.7974.
The difference is −0.0499, with a 95 % paired episode-bootstrap CI of [−0.7403, +0.6559] (X).
The term depends on the machine.
The same untrained network scored 1.4383 on one machine and 0.7974 and 0.8042 on two others.
It is sensitive to the BLAS library and to ridge conditioning.
The surprise monitor has a failure-class AUROC of 0.775, below its sanity bar.
We checked it for a loading or scoring bug.
The same scorer reproduces the open-loop corruption ratios at K = 30 (X).
Cross-episode gives 3.428, against 3.341 in the original run.
Constant-first gives 2.558, against 2.543.
We found no bug.
We ran an action-shuffle check on the predictor of VLA-JEPA at 5 anchors (Table @tab:vlajepa, from X).
Action tokens from another episode differ from the true ones by 21–28 % in relative L2.
They move the loss by about 0.05 %.
Zeroing the tokens moves it by about 1.05 % on average.
The forward pass is deterministic.
The predictor barely uses its actions.
Its failure-class AUROC is 0.501, below the same sanity check, and we leave its table unread under the frozen bar.
One pass in the register uses the imagined latent.
In the anticipation step of the outcome-readout gate, the imagined latent beat policy identity by +0.179.
That bar is retrospective.
We reran the same idea twice with the threshold committed first, in the grasp probe and in the calibrated surprise reflex.
Both fail.
LeWorldModel trains the recipe we use end to end from pixels and plans with it in Push-T and in simulation.
We tested its two planning uses on our arm, and both fail.
LeJEPA's identifiability analysis predicts that SIGReg latents identify the state up to anisotropy.
Our pose probes support this in part.
DINO-WM plans on frozen DINOv2 patches, and our frozen control uses the same design.
We timed V-JEPA 2.1 and RoboJEPA on our on-board computer, and both are too slow.
ContactGuard finds imagined-latent probes better than current-latent ones on grasp tasks.
On our arm we find the reverse.
We also re-tested ReAP's action-conditioned risk, the hierarchical planners of HWM and H-JEPA, and SURVEYOR's latent-distance scale.
All of them miss here, at this data scale.
SaiVLA-JEPA reports that a training-only future-latent head adds +0.03 points to control on 10,030 paired episodes.
HIJP finds LeWM below goal-conditioned behaviour cloning in simulation.
The split between encoder and predictor is exploratory.
We chose its probes after the data and fit them on 69 rollouts labelled by a single operator, the author.
The model never saw these rollouts, and every probe is cross-validated by session.
A fresh set of rollouts scored under a threshold committed first would confirm or reject the split.
That needs a day on the arm.
All results come from one model at one data scale.
A second point at 653 episodes is costed and queued.
We did not run three controls.
The surprise monitor and the imagined arm of the grasp probe would each need a predictor trained on frozen DINOv2-S features or on the joints.
Progress monotonicity with the controls would need a reimplementation.
In the register, the outcome-readout verdict is retrospective.
The two-level hierarchical progress use has its bar in the same commit as its result.
Ordered by commit alone, without the audit, the register reads 13 bar-first and 6 same-commit rows.
We tested 20 published uses on a $3.30 world model.
At this data scale the encoder reads the outcome and the predictor adds nothing to that reading.
In chunk ranking the commanded actions did better than the predictor, so they are worth keeping as a baseline for any model of this size.
Reward models that score robot rollouts are also used as failure detectors.
We compared two zero-shot reward models with plain episode length.
On ArmnetBench, a public SO-101 benchmark where runs end at a time limit, length separates failure from success at AUROC 0.942 within policy.
Failed runs are slow rather than cut off.
Length observed only up to half of the longest episode still gives 0.851.
Both reward models score below length, the better one at 0.821.
On our own rollouts an operator stopped each run by judgment.
There length falls to 0.56, and neither reward model beats the identity of the policy.
A judge that sees the finished episode passes its threshold, at an operating point chosen in-sample.
No mid-episode monitor reaches its bar.
The baseline a detector has to beat depends on the dataset's stopping rule.
Papers that evaluate a reward model as a failure detector normally compare it with other learned detectors.
When a benchmark stops failed runs at a time limit, the length of an episode also encodes its outcome.
The identity of the policy that ran can carry it too, and we call this the policy-identity null (mainly with models that give out-of-distribution results).
When the operator stops each run by his judgment, both signals are weaker.
We call the way a dataset ends its episodes its stopping rule.
None of the reward-model papers in our library reports the stopping rule or a length baseline.
We started with a narrower claim, that elapsed time is the reward model to beat.
Our own rollouts did not support it.
On them length is near chance, and a robot-trained judge passed its pre-registered threshold.
The stopping rule separates the two results, so it became the subject of the paper.
We measured length on ArmnetBench and on our own rollouts.
The length analyses were frozen before any number existed.
We compared length with two zero-shot reward models, Robometer and TOPReward.
On our 88 operator-stopped rollouts we also compared it with every judge and monitor we had run.
ArmnetBench v0.1 has 8 tasks and 7 policies on the SO-101.
We use its 2,047 policy rollouts with a success or failure class (515 successes, 1,532 failures).
We leave out the teleoperated episodes.
One task, pushing a Displayport cable (270 rollouts), has rollouts of a single class and so no per-task AUROC.
Our own data are 88 labelled bowls-task episodes on one SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX.
Every monitor gate used the same 50-episode subset (42 successes, 8 failures).
The author was the operator.
He stopped each run and labelled it at rest, not blind to the policy.
On ArmnetBench, episode length is a strong failure detector within each policy (Table 1, Fig. 1).
Pooled over policies it reaches 0.938.
Within each policy it ranges from 0.91 to 0.96.
Pair-weighted, the within-policy value is 0.942, with a CI of 0.927–0.956.
We ran Robometer-4B zero-shot, as its authors ship it.
It scores 0.818 pooled and 0.821 within policy.
The within-policy value is pair-weighted over its per-policy scores, and their range stands in for a CI (§7).
We ran TOPReward with Qwen3-VL-8B and no training.
It scores 0.661 within policy.
Its paired difference to length has a 95 % CI of -0.31 to -0.25.
The protocols fixed each model's primary score before any score existed.
For Robometer it is the success probability, and for TOPReward the success score of its paper.
Two other scores from the same runs are in Table 1 as descriptive rows.
They are higher, and still below length.
We take each task's longest episode as its timeout.
Only 8.7 % of failures run that long.
At half that length, 88 % of failures are still running.
Only 19 % of successes are.
Length observed up to that cut gives 0.851 within policy (CI 0.829–0.873; Fig. 2).
TOPReward on frames up to the same cut reaches 0.667.
Failed rollouts are slow, not timed out.
Both readings fixed in the protocol hold.
On our own operator-stopped rollouts, length is at chance.
It gives 0.56 on the 69 rollouts TOPReward scored and 0.52 on all 88.
Here the policy-identity null is the baseline to beat.
17 of the 25 failures in the 69 come from one policy, TurboVLA.
Neither reward model beats policy identity.
TOPReward scores 0.82 (CI 0.70–0.93), and policy identity alone 0.87.
On the 50 episodes without TurboVLA, TOPReward scores 0.78.
Robometer scores 0.577 on all 88, and policy identity 0.878.
We first ran a deterministic top-camera check (colour masks and geometry, no learning).
It is right on 94.3 % of judged episodes.
It has 0 false positives (Wilson 0–13 %) and 5 false negatives.
We then gave Flora-Rewarder-27B a 64-frame two-view clip and NVIDIA's prompt.
It reaches a threshold-free AUROC of 1.00 (bootstrap CI 1.00–1.00).
At its in-sample operating point it flags 8 of 8 failures at 2 of 42 successes (Wilson on the false alarms 1–16 %).
The pre-registered bar was at least 6 of 8 failures at no more than 2 of 42 successes, so it passes.
Its base model, Qwen3.5-27B, has no robot fine-tune.
On the same input it also passes, with AUROC 0.91 (0.78–1.00) and 7 of 8 at 2 of 42.
The input format mattered more than the fine-tune.
Qwen3.5-9B flags 16 successes and fails.
Gemini 3.8 Flash fails by one false alarm.
The bar for mid-episode monitors is at least 5 of 8 failures at no more than 1 of 20 false interventions.
No monitor reaches it on these 50 rollouts (Fig. 3).
The surprise of a separate world model, trained in the LeWorldModel recipe, catches 2 of 8 at 2 of 42 (AUROC 0.86).
A Gemini sliding-window judge catches 0.
We also built an action-conditioned risk head on the world model's latent.
Its first version reached AUROC 0.93.
It read elapsed time, so we withdrew that result.
We pre-registered a second version without time or length.
It catches 3 of 8 at 5 of 42.
Its AUROC is 0.79, and 0.71 with shuffled actions.
The MLP variant catches 6 of 8 and flags 13 of 42.
Robometer scales a general-purpose reward model through trajectory comparisons.
TOPReward reads the token probabilities of a video-language model as hidden rewards.
A survey of verifiers for robot policies covers the wider family.
FAIL-Detect and SAFE learn uncertainty- and feature-based failure scores for imitation and VLA policies.
FARM reads failure signals from the internal states of a frozen world model, like our world-model monitors.
ReAP predicts action-conditioned risk, and our risk head follows it.
VLA-Corrector verifies stages, Spotter adds a reflecting VLM, and REMORA tracks progress through errors and recovery.
ArmnetBench and a standardized SO-101 VLA benchmark evaluate policies on the same arm.
None of these works reports the elapsed-length baseline under the dataset's stopping rule.
The judge pass on our own rollouts rests on 8 failures.
Its operating thresholds were chosen on the same 50 episodes.
A single operator, the author, labelled them and was not blind to the policy.
The threshold-free AUROCs do not depend on the threshold.
Fresh rollouts scored at the frozen thresholds would confirm the operating points.
17 of the 25 failures in our 69 rollouts are TurboVLA's.
Any score that reads the policy therefore gets the policy-identity null for free.
The risk head is trained and tested on the same 50 episodes.
Five folds by episode keep episodes from leaking, but tasks and policies leak.
Robometer's per-episode scores stayed on an older machine.
Its within-policy number therefore has no episode-bootstrap CI, and it is missing from the truncation analysis.
A copy from that machine or a re-score of about $6 would restore both.
TOPReward's paper does not give its prefix count, frames per query or Yes/No wording, so those are our choices.
The ArmnetBench result covers eight tasks.
The timeout is approximated by each task's longest episode.
On ArmnetBench, where runs end at a time limit, episode length beat both reward models.
On our operator-stopped rollouts length was at chance, and a judge that saw the whole finished episode caught the failures.
When you evaluate a reward model as a failure detector, report episode length within policy on the same rows and say how the episodes ended.
We re-measured seven training-free methods for action chunking in flow-matching VLAs.
Their papers report numbers from desktop GPUs.
We ran them where a low-cost robot runs its policy, with SmolVLA on a Jetson Orin NX.
All tests share one checkpoint and the same recorded episodes.
Each test had its threshold committed before the run, and every number traces to a result file and a protocol commit.
On this board the vision encoder takes 151.0 of 219.0 ms of server time per chunk (25 W).
The two methods that act on the seam between chunks pass.
A gradient-free prefix overwrite cuts the boundary jump by 72 % or more.
Movement-primitive seam conditioning removes most of the seam jerk.
The sampling methods do not transfer. vla.cpp samples in sequence, so every N-sample method pays for N chunks one after another.
Multiple training-free chunking tricks for flow-matching VLAs have come out this year.
Their numbers always come from strong desktop or data-centre GPUs (RTX 4090, A100, H100, RTX 5090).
On these, a chunk costs barely tens of milliseconds and spare compute is plentiful.
A robot people can buy runs its policy on an edge GPU.
There most of the chunk goes to the vision encoder, which these tricks don't affect.
We measured how much of each trick is left on such a board.
Our robot is an SO-101 arm [arXiv:2606.08881] with a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB.
It runs SmolVLA [arXiv:2506.01844] through vla.cpp, a C++ inference engine, on episodes recorded with LeRobot.
This paper started once SmolVLA ran on the arm through vla.cpp.
We then looked at where the rest of a chunk's time went, and at which published tricks could still help.
We took seven of them.
Each one is a gate with a bar committed before the number.
Offline effects get an episode bootstrap, and latencies are medians of at least 50 calls.
The appendix maps every number to its result file and protocol commit.
We follow one chunk of ten Euler steps at full power (MAXN_SUPER).
It costs 237.5 ms end to end (Fig. 1).
Vision takes 150.7 ms and prefill 14.9 ms.
Each denoise step takes 5.3 ms.
At 25 W the server-side split is 151.0 ms of vision in 219.0 ms.
A trick that only touches the denoising loop works on at most a quarter of the chunk.
Two power modes appear in this paper.
Each gate's protocol froze the mode it ran in.
The serving split and the boundary experiments ran at 25 W, and the latency experiments at full power.
Every number below carries its mode.
Two tricks act on the seam between chunks, and both pass.
The first overwrites the new chunk's executed prefix with the actions already committed.
It passes the 50 % jump-cut bar at every delay, in PyTorch and in vla.cpp.
In vla.cpp it adds 0.4 ms per chunk.
The second is movement-primitive chunking [arXiv:2610.39451].
Projecting each chunk onto ten Gaussian bases keeps the error within its bar and removes within-chunk jerk.
Conditioning on the last action sent removes 83–87 % of the seam jerk at +0.19° of error.
Its paper reports 73–84 %.
We measured on the commanded stream only.
Cutting the Euler steps from ten to two [arXiv:2610.32102] saves 41 ms per chunk at full power.
The vision cost is much larger.
The paper claims that the action cloud contracts around an unchanged centroid.
It reports a cloud ratio of 0.51 on π0.
Our ratio is 0.78.
It falls between the bar of 0.70 and the fail line of 0.85, so the claim is not proven here.
The paper also expects fewer steps to remove edge-GPU thermal throttling.
Our Orin did not throttle at ten steps in either power mode.
We keep ten steps, as the protocol says while the contraction is unproven.
Two tricks sample several chunks per decision.
Speculative chunk selection [arXiv:2610.28019] samples four candidates.
It uses the pre-commit frame to pick the one closest to the recorded teleoperation continuation.
Offline it beats a random pick (one continuation per frame, training-set episodes, open loop).
Its paper promises no added control-step delay.
On the Orin, vla.cpp samples the candidates in sequence.
A cycle costs 1,200 ms and 37 control ticks, against 8 for a naive chunk (Fig. 3).
Entropy-adaptive chunk length [arXiv:2604.04161] samples 20 chunks per decision.
One decision takes 4,751 ms on the Orin.
The threshold was 298 ms.
